reason: The registry contract is kept as package delegate/jobs: job types, owner-fenced calls, the two session records and the jobs projection. Changes: no unowned jobs, kinds are registered as effects, producers push output, and the model read is Peek then Commit.

The in-process registry is kept as component jobs.registry: admission before start, one bounded ring per job, first-wins settlement. Go adds a stop grace that forces settlement, settlement before the owner's final flush, a cap on settled records and closing of jobs lost with the host.

The three model tools, the controller and completion notices are kept as component tool.jobs. Notice delivery becomes one waking send with a refilling wake budget, and the unread output stays in the registry until the notice is claimed.

Host-owned schedules with seven timing kinds, three targets, latest-only catch-up and bounded history are kept as component schedule.service. Storage becomes two typed tables in the home database, and firing uses a per-occurrence claim plus a deterministic message id so that several processes on one home deliver once.

The four schedule tools stay a per-preset consumer of the host service. Go adds enforced rules: a session sees only its own schedules, a mutation needs a human turn or an approval, and a delegated agent is not shown the tools.

Event-sourced goal state with whole-value goal/change events, a strict fold, compare-and-set mutations and in-memory arming is kept as component goal.service. The state gains optional token and time budgets.

The driver that opens one follow-up turn per round at idle, with a reservation and a pre-step fence, is kept as component goal.rounds. Automatic stops become logged blockers with codes, and budgets plus a bounded retry of transient failures are added.
get_goal, create_goal and update_goal are kept with the same arguments and the same execution-time authority rules (human turn on a root agent, or the exact goal round for terminal reports).

The /goal command and its grammar are kept as component command.goal. Every operation is also a plain service call, so the server-rendered goal panel, the SDK protocol and the command line reach it without the command registry.

Logged per-agent plan state, the guidance section, /plan and the reviewed exit_plan_mode tool are kept as component plan.mode. Go changes soft guidance into an enforced read-only mode, appends the state at once and captures it per step.

Same name and arguments (job_id, wait, timeout_ms). Returns output since the last read and a status line, exclusive, bounded by the ring size, the producer's output limit and the pipeline ceiling; a wait ends on settlement, timeout or the shared steer watch.
Same name, no arguments. Lists the caller's jobs one per line, parallel-safe, bounded to the per-owner live limit plus the settled-record cap with labels cut at 120 characters.

Same name and arguments (job_id, reason). Requests cancellation and returns one snapshot; the job settles when its producer has returned or the stop grace has passed. Declared with direct reach only and denied in plan mode.

Same name; arguments title, prompt, rrule and target, plus an optional expire_after_seconds. Changed: allowed only in a human turn or after an approval, bounded by per-session and per-home caps and a prompt size limit, and the result says whether a firing host is live.
Same name and arguments. Changed: it lists only schedules the calling session created or receives, returns summaries without prompt bodies, and its page limit is 20 by default and 100 at most.
Same name and argument. Changed: scoped to the caller's schedules, and the result adds host time, the next occurrence and the last five deliveries with their state.
Same name; update, pause, resume or delete with a compare-and-set revision. Changed: scoped and authorised like schedule_create, and a delete reports whether a still-queued message was retracted.
Same name and result: the current goal as compact JSON or null. The objective is bounded by maxObjectiveBytes.
Same name and arguments (objective, max_goal_rounds). Exclusive, direct reach only, allowed only in a human turn on a root agent, as upstream.

Same name, actions and compare-and-set arguments. Authority rules are kept; a completion may additionally be rejected by a goal.Completing listener, and a terminal report from a goal round adds the closing instruction to its result.

Same name and argument (a Markdown plan starting with a heading), offered once plan mode has been active. It opens a typed plan-review interaction; approve, keep planning, dismiss, no reviewer and interruption each have a defined result. The plan is bounded by maxPlanBytes.
Replaced one for one by the typed notify key goal.Changed, dispatched through the agent's scope after the goal/change append, carrying the operation, the reference and the view.
Replaced one for one by the typed notify key goal.ActivationChanged with the session, the goal reference and whether it is armed; the goal panel's live fragment consumes it.
Replaced by the typed notify key schedule.Changed, which carries the changed ids and whether the change was made by this process or seen from another through the revision counter.

Upstream lets the embedding activate a target session through a waterfall. Go uses a service interface, schedule.Activator, provided by the carrier that keeps sessions loaded, with a fallback in the schedule component; a service cannot be shadowed by listener order and returns a release function.

Go struct local.Config: maxConcurrentJobsPerOwner 10, retainBytes 262144, settledRetainBytes 16384 as upstream, plus maxSettledPerOwner 50 and stopGrace 10s. pumpPollMs is dropped because producers push output.

Go struct jobtools.Config: waitTimeout 30s, maxWaitTimeout 10m, completionDelivery and inlineOutputBytes 2048 as upstream; maxConsecutiveWakes becomes finite by default (50) and wakeRefillInterval (10m) is new.

Go struct schedule.Config keeps deliveryHistoryDays 30, deliveryHistoryRecords 200 and the new-session interval, and adds fire, wakeCap 30s, caps on active schedules, per-session schedules, prompt bytes and concurrently created sessions, and the delivery retry policy.
Go struct goal.Config: defaultMaxRounds 256 as upstream, plus defaultMaxTokens, defaultMaxDuration (both none by default) and maxObjectiveBytes.
Go struct goaltools.Config with blockedAfterConsecutiveRounds 3 as upstream. The round driver, which has no config upstream, gets rounds.Config for retry and consecutive budget rounds.
Go struct plan.Config: section stays required and non-empty and unknown keys stay a load error; enforcement (read-only by default), allowTools and maxPlanBytes are new.
ctx.jobs becomes service key jobs.Key with interface jobs.Registry (Start, List, Get, Peek, Commit, ReadAt, Kill, Wait, Remove, Subscribe, RegisterKind, AttachController).

ctx.schedule becomes service key schedule.Key with interface schedule.Service (Create, Edit, Get, List, History, RunNow, Status); every method takes the caller so that scoping is enforced in the service.
ctx.goals becomes service key goal.Key with interface goal.Service (Get, Create, Update, Disarm); mutations name an exact id and revision and carry the caller's authority.

ctx.planMode becomes service key plan.Key with interface plan.Controller (Get, Set); the state it returns distinguishes the logged value, the value captured for the open step and whether plan mode was ever active.

The Go contract is still in-process: Spec.Run is a Go function and the registry lives in the host. Identity is already restart-stable (a UUID-based job id and an agent reference), but live work cannot be handed to another process.
justification: A job's producer holds process handles, pipes and in-process state; re-attaching after the host died needs a supervisor process outside the host, which this design does not have. DH-ADR-JOBS-1 states the limit and DH-ADR-JOBS-4 records the loss in the session log.

reason: The model cursor stays the only consuming read; observers use ReadAt at their own offset. Go only splits the consuming read into Peek and Commit.
justification: Deliberate: one model, one cursor. Two consuming readers would each receive part of the output. Kept by DH-ADR-JOBS-2.

reason: The registry keeps at most maxSettledPerOwner settled records per owner (default 50) and removes the oldest collected one first, so the listed set is bounded without an explicit remove.
Jobs and their output rings still end with the host process. On resume each lost job is closed in the log with cause host-exit and the model is told; spilled output survives, ring output does not.
justification: No supervisor process exists outside the host to keep or re-attach to a producer's processes and pipes. DH-ADR-JOBS-1 keeps jobs in-process; DH-ADR-JOBS-4 and DH-D-JOBS-2 make the loss a recorded fact.

reason: A job is an effect of its owner's scope fiber, so teardown cancels it and appends job/settled inside the scope unwind, which the agent teardown order places before the final bounded flush and the lease release. A hard kill is the crash path: resume appends the settlement with cause host-exit.

Cancellation is the context of a blocking Run function. If Run has not returned after stopGrace the registry settles the job as failed with producerReported false, frees its capacity slot and lists the goroutine as detached, so a silent cancel can neither stall teardown nor hold a slot.

The notice is one waking steer; the sender never decides whether the owner is busy. The Go inbox makes a waking send either land in the running turn or open a new one, so there is no window in which a notice is queued and nothing wakes.
The notice peeks the unread output and the registry commits the model cursor only when the driver claims the message. Nothing is held in the tools component, so reloading it loses no output.
The wake budget refills by one wake per wakeRefillInterval as well as on a user message, and a notice held past the budget raises a live jobs.NoticeHeld notice so the UI can show that one is waiting.

The jobs projection derives from the log which settlements the model was never given (no claimed notice, no terminal job_output). On resume one notice names them, so a notice discarded at disposal is not the last word.
The model tools remain the single consuming reader of a job's stream; the UI follows a job through the non-consuming ReadAt.
justification: Deliberate, same cause as the registry's one model cursor: a second consuming reader would split the output between readers. Kept by DH-ADR-JOBS-2.

reason: Unowned jobs are not built: every job has an owning agent reference and Start refuses a spec without one. Host work that belongs to no session is an ordinary fiber effect, not a job.

The release decision leaves the tool: package delegate/steer keeps one subscription per agent and closes a channel when a message of source kind user is queued for the current step. The spec also asks the agent area to reserve the user kind to carrier entry points, so a component cannot label its own input as a steer.

The steer watch is shared: Registry.Wait takes a context, and job_output and any other blocking wait (the subagent area's wait tools) select on the same per-agent channel instead of each copying the release logic.

A schedule still fires only while a process that fires schedules is running. The retry part of the limit is removed: a failed delivery retries with back-off and pauses with a reason after maxDeliveryAttempts, any firing host on the home can deliver, and a late delivery reports how late it is and how many occurrences were missed.
justification: The harness installs no operating-system service or daemon; it is one binary that runs when started. DH-ADR-JOBS-7 narrows the limit and states it; DH-ADR-JOBS-6 defines catch-up.

reason: The message id is derived from schedule, occurrence and generation and the inbox refuses a duplicate, so a send repeated after a crash is a no-op and the inbox gets the message once. The delivery row then follows the message to ran or discarded, and a message discarded by disposal is delivered once more.

Hard delete is kept as a decision, but what was delivered stays recoverable: every delivered message is a logged user message whose source names the schedule and occurrence. The part about version 1 session-log reminders does not arise, because the Go store reads no upstream data.

Every service method takes a caller. An agent caller reads and changes only schedules it created or receives; only an owner principal admitted by a carrier manages all of them; a delegated agent is refused in the service as well as in the tools.

The rule languages stay bounded (five-field cron, the RFC 5545 subset of the recurrence library spec) and future occurrences still depend on the zone data of the machine. Committed occurrences are stored as UTC and never move.
justification: The subset is deliberate (DH-ADR-RRULE-1) and zone rules are changed by governments, so no design removes the dependency. DH-ADR-JOBS-6 states both limits and DH-ADR-TEMPORAL-1 reports the data source.

reason: Schedules are rows with indexed status, next occurrence, target and creator; history is a separate table read by page. Nothing is loaded wholesale at open, a write touches one row, and list results are summaries without prompt bodies.

The 60 second floor and latest-only catch-up are kept as stated rules. What was missing is added: maxConcurrentNewSessions caps sessions created by schedules, and each late delivery carries the missed count and its lateness.

Recovery no longer inspects the latest receipt's session: a stale claim is taken over and the deterministic message id makes the repeat a no-op. Change notices are derived, not pushed: at a turn's first step the tools component compares the session's schedules with the revisions its model last saw and injects one notice, loaded or not at the time of the change.

tool.schedule declares schedule.Key as a required service; a composition that mounts the tools without the service shows the entry as waiting on that named service in the loader's status and in the composed-tree preview, which is what outcome DH-O-2 requires.

The tool pipeline attributes every call to an agent at its first stage, and the service takes an explicit caller; a call with no agent is refused with the classified schedule/no-caller error instead of an internal error.

The tools reach only schedules the calling session created or receives, and a create or edit outside a human turn returns Ask, so a person approves or, with no answerer, it is denied. The check is in the service and the pipeline, not in a prompt sentence.

Delete and pause remove a delivered message that no turn has claimed yet from the target's inbox when this process holds the session. When another process holds it the message stays and the result says retracted false.

schedule_view returns the host's current time, the next occurrence and the last deliveries with their state (enqueued, ran with its turn, discarded, skipped, failed) and attempt count, so the model can see timing, retries and whether a delivery ran.
The refusal of a delegated caller is kept and moved to where it cannot be skipped: the service refuses an agent caller with a delegation depth above zero, whichever tool or entry made the call.
The four declarations carry a step-time condition that is false for a delegated agent, so a child's requests do not contain the schemas or the authorization section and pay no tokens for them.

The split is kept on purpose (state in component goal), and the missing policies now exist as a deliverable: component goal.rounds decides when a goal continues, retries transient failures within a bound and cancels the running turn on a host pause.
A goal may carry a token budget and a time budget beside its round cap. Both are derived from the log, and the driver records a blocker with code token-budget or time-budget when one runs out.

The caller that records completion or blocking is still authoritative. Go adds one interception, goal.Completing, through which a deployment can reject a completion with a deterministic check; no evaluator ships.
justification: An independent evaluator is a second model judging the first, with its own cost, prompt and trust questions that no upstream behaviour defines. DH-ADR-JOBS-10 keeps the model as judge and provides the place where a check attaches.

reason: A session still has at most one current goal and there is no goal database; history stays in the session log.
justification: Deliberate: a goal is one objective of one session. Parallel objectives are separate sessions or delegated agents, which the delegation areas own. Kept by DH-ADR-JOBS-9.

reason: No third-party code runs in the host: a plugin is a separate process that cannot append session events of a host-owned type. Inside the host the typed append handle for goal/change is private to package goal. The strict fold is kept as the last check.
The model still decides when evidence is sufficient and whether a blocker is unchanged; the runtime enforces only counts. A goal.Completing listener may veto a completion.
justification: Same cause as the goal service's limit: no evaluator is defined upstream and designing one is a separate feature. DH-ADR-JOBS-10 records the choice.

reason: Rounds run in the same session. The driver starts no fresh agent and forks nothing.
justification: Deliberate boundary: independent attempts with fresh context are delegation and workflows, owned by the subagent and workflow areas. DH-ADR-JOBS-9 keeps a goal to one session.

reason: The Go port releases a fiber's effects one at a time, newest first. The driver registers its pre-step fence first and its remove-my-prompt-and-disarm effect last, so on unload the queued round prompt is removed and every goal disarmed before the fence goes; no accepted prompt can start a round unfenced.

Token and time budgets are part of the goal, and the turn budget is mapped: a round ending on it counts, and a configured run of such rounds blocks the goal with code turn-budget. Each automatic stop is a blocker code, so resource limits are attributed to the goal.

A round whose turn failed with a failure the model-provider area classes as transient is retried after back-off, at most retryFailedRounds times, then the goal is blocked with code provider-failure. A failed flush is never retried: it disarms.
Execution proves that the turn holds a direct human message on a root agent, not that the request merits a goal; that stays the model's judgement.
justification: Intent cannot be checked mechanically, and asking a person to confirm every goal would remove the tool's purpose. DH-ADR-JOBS-9 keeps the human-turn test and states what it does not prove.

reason: The runtime enforces the number of consecutive rounds before a model-reported blocker, not that the obstacle is the same one.
justification: Semantic equivalence of obstacles needs an evaluator, which is not designed (DH-ADR-JOBS-10). The count threshold bounds the harm of a wrong judgement.

reason: The tools still only change state, and the two consumers the bullet names are separate deliverables of this spec: the round driver schedules, and the command and the server-rendered goal panel show the goal to a person.

The guidance about goal rounds is contributed by the goal.rounds component, so a composition that mounts the tools without the driver does not teach the model a path that cannot occur; the human-turn operations work without the driver.

A prompt section of this area is rendered only when at least one of its tools is in the step view of the requesting agent, so hiding the tools hides the guidance. The same rule is used for the job and schedule sections.

The Go UI is server-rendered HTML: the goal panel is a form (objective, round cap, a confirmation before replacing) that calls the goal service directly, so editing does not depend on a text command registry. The /goal command stays as a text shortcut.
The service's create and edit requests carry the round cap and the budgets for any human caller; the panel shows them as fields, so a person sets them without asking the model.
The goal projection and the goal.ActivationChanged notice drive a live fragment on the event stream, so the current phase, round count and arming are shown continuously and survive a reconnect.

Goal operations are service calls, not only a command: the spec asks the SDK protocol, the command line and the HTTP routes to expose get, create, edit, pause, resume and clear, so headless and automation clients control a goal without a command adapter.

Plan mode is enforced by default: a deny-only guard refuses every tool with effects, commands run only under a read-only sandbox ceiling and are denied where the ceiling cannot be applied. Guidance-only behaviour remains as a configuration choice.

A selection is appended to the log as plan/mode when it is made, with or without an open turn, and takes effect at the next proposed step. Nothing waits in process memory, so nothing is lost when the process exits.
Creation takes a plan option, and a subagent created while its creator is in plan mode starts in plan mode with origin inherited, so delegation cannot be used to write during planning.
A subagent in plan mode is not offered exit_plan_mode and returns its plan as its result to the parent that asked.
justification: Deliberate: a child's plan is reviewed by its parent, which presents it to the person; a second review channel per child would put several reviews before one person with no order. Kept by DH-ADR-JOBS-11.

reason: The review is an interaction of kind plan-review with the plan as a typed payload, so every carrier that can answer an interaction (browser, SDK, command line) can show the plan and the two choices; no client-only presentation is involved.

Read in full. Kept: goal state is its own whole-value goal/change event appended by the goal service, the fold reads only that event for lifecycle state, a goal-sourced user message only advances the round count, and arming is never persisted.
summary: Goal state is a durable goal/change event carrying the whole snapshot, not something encoded in an inbox message.

reason: Read in full. Kept: one ring per job, a model cursor and offset reads, one projection, one filtered event stream, caller-scoped operations. Two changes: pull sources and their pump are replaced by pushed appends, and the notice ledger's held read moves into the registry as Peek and Commit.
summary: One output ring, one projection and one event stream per background job, with two cursors over one storage.

reason: Read in full. Kept: schedules are host storage that outlives sessions, storage is authoritative and a failure is never read as no tasks, inbox persistence precedes the receipt. Changed: the whole-unit document becomes typed rows, fail closed applies per row, a retry policy exists, and version 1 reading is not needed.
summary: Scheduled messages live in host-owned storage, survive restart, and an unreadable store is a load failure.

reason: Read in full. Kept: targets session, new_once and new; the session id reserved before each create attempt; latest-only catch-up; the 60 second floor; one execution slot for a reused target. Change notices become derived at turn start instead of pushed to loaded agents only.
summary: Three delivery targets, session ids reserved before creation, latest-only catch-up and a per-task delivery floor.

reason: Read in full. Kept: delete removes the row and its delivery records with no deleted state, and history is bounded by age (30 days) and count (200) on the only write path, always keeping the latest record.
summary: Hard delete of schedules and delivery history bounded by age and count.

reason: Read in full. Kept: the model tools are a separate component mounted per preset over a host-wide service, so a preset without them pays no tokens. The note's host-wide reach of the tools is narrowed to the caller's own schedules.
summary: Schedule tools are a preset-level consumer; the schedule service stays host-wide.

reason: Read in full. Kept: a fixed origin line and no instruction to distrust the payload. Refined: the line says who wrote the prompt (the user, or the assistant in a named session), and the message's source kind is schedule and never user, so authority checks cannot mistake it for a person.
summary: A delivered reminder opens with a fixed line stating it is a scheduled message; the untrusted wording was removed.

reason: Read in full. Kept: one schedule store, seven timing kinds evaluated normally, cron and recurrence rules authoritative in their stored text, parsing and arithmetic in the shared time package. Not carried: version 1 read compatibility, because the Go store reads no upstream data.
summary: One schedule storage domain in which cron and recurrence rules are ordinary timing kinds.

reason: Read in full. Kept: job/registered and job/settled facts with owner, kind, label, tool call and a UUID-based id; producerReported; a failed append never blocks cleanup. Extended: settlement is appended before the owner's final flush, and a resumed session closes jobs the host lost with cause host-exit instead of leaving them incomplete.
summary: Owned jobs append registered and settled facts to the session log; a failed journal append never blocks cleanup.

reason: Read in full. Kept: three exclusive tools, compare-and-set on id and revision, execution-time authority (human turn on a root agent; the exact goal round for complete and blocked), the blocked threshold, the wrap-up instruction, and resume of a paused goal reserved for the user.
summary: get_goal, create_goal and update_goal with compare-and-set updates and execution-time authority checks.

reason: Read in full. Kept: archive admission is answered from stored rows, not from a live agent, so an idle session with active schedules refuses the archive. Changed: a stop pauses those schedules with reason target-archived instead of deleting them, because an archive can be undone.
summary: Archive admission for schedules reads stored task rows; a stop removes them in one batch.

reason: Read in full. Kept for this area: the schedule accepts no implicit zone; an absolute time has an explicit offset or a named zone, a gap is rejected, an overlap takes the earlier instant, and only a UTC instant is stored. Sampling the browser's zone per prompt belongs to the context and composer areas.
summary: No session time-zone state; schedule inputs carry an explicit offset or zone.

reason: Read in full. The proposal is not built upstream and is not designed here: source providers, the trigger layer and run records are deferred. Two of its rules are adopted now: the schedule row has a source discriminator whose only value is time, and host-delivered content never has source kind user. This overrules the first verdict of ported.
summary: Proposal: automation tasks with pluggable sources, a model-free trigger layer and event content quoted as data.

title: A job is owned by one session's agent and lives in the host process
One bounded ring per job, pushed appends, and a two-phase model cursor
Completion notices use one waking send, a refilling wake budget and a shared steer watch
A job settles when its producer has returned or a grace has passed, and the record is durable before the lease goes
Schedules are rows in two typed tables of the home database
Time rules: explicit zones, wall time or elapsed time by kind, latest-only catch-up, a 30 second wake cap
A due occurrence is claimed in the database, delivered by a process that can write the target, and sent under a deterministic message id
The model may schedule only for its own session, only when a person asked, and within caps
A goal is one event-sourced objective per session, changed by compare-and-set, and never armed by a restart
A round is a turn; a goal ends by a closed set of logged reasons; budgets and a bounded retry are built in
Plan mode is enforced read-only, logged at once, captured per step, and left by a reviewed plan
Event-triggered automation is deferred; the schedule row keeps a source field
Long-running work is registered, bounded and observable through one registry
Every job leaves a start and an end in its session's log, also across teardown and a crash
The model reads, lists and stops its jobs and is told when one finishes
Schedules are stored durably and their times are computed by stated rules
A due schedule is delivered once, by one process, also when several share the home
The model manages schedules for its own session under an enforced authority rule
A session remembers one goal, and people and the model change it through one checked service
An armed goal keeps working round by round and stops for a recorded reason
In plan mode the agent can read but not change, and leaves only through a reviewed plan
Job admission checks refuse with their own codes and leave nothing behind; owner fence
Output ring bounds, UTF-8 safe trimming, lossy reads, observer reads and Peek then Commit
Kill, first-wins settlement, forced settlement after the stop grace, and the settled-record cap
Job facts are appended in order, settlement precedes the owner's final flush, and a failed append blocks nothing
A resumed session closes jobs lost with the host once, with cause host-exit and one notice
The three job tools: results, bounds, single consumption, scheduling class and wait clamp
Completion notices: which settlements notify, inline or pointer, commit on claim, no stranded notice, reload loses nothing
The wake budget is spent and refilled, quiet never wakes, and the steer watch releases every waiter on a user message only
Schedule row codec is strict; an undecodable row is invalid and inert; an unreadable table fails the component
The time-rule table across daylight-saving gaps and overlaps, including elapsed-time minute rules and wildcard-hour cron
Catch-up delivers the latest occurrence once with a missed count and lateness; exhaustion, expiry and a clock moved back
Delivery history is pruned by count and age, delete is hard, and a stale revision is a conflict
The wake loop respects the cap, recomputes on local and foreign changes, and decides due by the clock at waking
Two instances race for one occurrence: one claim wins, a dead holder's claim is taken over, a stale epoch is refused
A fault between send and receipt yields one message and one delivery row after takeover
Targets: reserved ids are reused, missing or archived targets pause, a foreign holder defers, retries back off and then pause
Delivery state follows the message to ran or discarded; one redelivery after disposal; delete retracts an unclaimed message
The schedule activity provider reports active schedules for a session and a stop pauses exactly those
The four schedule tools: schemas, bounded results, scoping to the caller, and absence for a delegated agent
Schedule authority through the executor and the tool command line: human turn, schedule-woken turn, Ask, no answerer, caps
Goal fold: legal transitions, stale revision, corrupt records, clear tombstone, disarmed after resume and fork
Goal tool authority matrix, the blocked threshold, and resume of a paused goal refused for the model
The /goal grammar, and every goal operation reachable as a service call without the command registry
Goal rounds in virtual time: idle opens one round, human input wins, stale rounds are rejected, cap, cancel, disposal, unload order
Goal budgets and retry: turn-budget rounds, token and time budgets, bounded retry, flush failure, a rejected completion
Plan state is appended at once, captured per step, and the exit tool is offered from the first active step onward
Plan enforcement through the executor and the tool command line: effects denied, reads allowed, commands only under the read-only ceiling
Plan review outcomes, plan validation, inheritance by subagents and the creation option
A real background command is read, stopped and accounted for across a host kill
Two real processes on one home deliver a due schedule once
A schedule a real model created fires after downtime, once, and cannot multiply
A real model works a goal over several rounds and stops for a recorded reason
Plan mode stops a real model from writing until a person approves in a real browser
A zoned schedule works on a machine with no zone database
